overview.title: From unigrams to bigrams: adding local word order
overview.main_topic: Motivating n-grams and building a multi-hot encoding over a joint unigram + bigram vocabulary with TextVectorization(ngrams=2)
overview.central_idea: Discarding all word order loses meaning carried by multi-word expressions ("United States", "not bad"). A cheap fix that keeps the set-based model is to treat pairs of consecutive tokens (bigrams) as extra vocabulary terms. TextVectorization does this out of the box with ngrams=2 and a larger 30,000-term vocabulary.
overview.importance: This is the step from a pure bag-of-words (unigram) model to an n-gram model. It raises test accuracy from 88% to 90% (p.428) and leads into the limits of n-grams that motivate sequence models (p.428-429).
learning_objectives: Explain why discarding word order loses information, using "United States" and "not bad"
Define unigram, bigram and n-gram, and list the unigrams and bigrams of "this movie made me cry"
Compare a bigram-only vocabulary with a shared unigram + bigram vocabulary
Read listing 14.16 and explain the roles of max_tokens=30_000, split, output_mode and ngrams=2
Explain why the vocabulary must be re-adapted
prerequisites: Listing 14.12 (p.423): TextVectorization with multi-hot output and adapt()
The bag-of-words model and its 88% test accuracy (p.424-426)

summary:
Section 14.4.2 starts by admitting the main weakness of the bag-of-words model: **discarding all word order is very reductive**. Some concepts span several words. "United States" means something quite different from "united" and "states" taken separately, and a movie that is "not bad" should get a different sentiment score from one that is "bad".

The fix keeps the simple set-based model but injects **local** word order through **bigrams**, pairs of consecutive tokens. For "this movie made me cry" the **unigrams** are `{"this", "movie", "made", "me", "cry"}` and the bigrams are `{"this movie", "movie made", "made me", "me cry"}`. The model just trained is therefore a *unigram model*, and an **n-gram** is an ordered sequence of n tokens.

To add bigrams, bigram frequencies are counted while building the vocabulary. You can either build a vocabulary of bigrams only, or let unigrams and bigrams **compete for the same vocabulary slots** by frequency. In that case "United States" would enter the vocabulary before "ventriloquism" if it occurs more often.

The authors could extend their `WordTokenizer` but don't need to: **`TextVectorization` supports this out of the box**. **Listing 14.16** raises `max_tokens` to **30,000** to make room for bigrams, keeps `split="whitespace"` and `output_mode="multi_hot"`, adds **`ngrams=2`** (the callout says this "considers all unigrams and bigrams"), re-runs `adapt()` on the unlabeled training texts, and maps the layer over the train, validation and test datasets with `num_parallel_calls=8`, producing `bigram_train_ds`, `bigram_val_ds` and `bigram_test_ds`. The page ends by announcing an inspection of a preprocessed batch, shown on p.428.

paragraphs.excerpt: Of course, we can intuitively guess that discarding all word order is very reductive
paragraphs.what_it_says: Throwing away all word order is very reductive, because even atomic concepts can take several words. "United States" means something different from "states" and "united" separately, and "not bad" and "bad" should get different sentiment scores.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A unigram model sums one weight per word present. For "not bad" it adds w("not") + w("bad"); since "bad" is strongly negative, the review is pushed toward negative even though the phrase is mildly positive. Negation and compound names are interactions between neighbouring words, which a model that is additive over single words can't represent.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It names the failure mode that bigrams target and, later, that sequence models address more fully.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in a linear model over unigrams, the contribution of each word is independent of context. Adding the bigram feature "not bad" gives the model its own weight for the phrase, which can override the sum of the separate word weights.

terminology.meaning: The sequence in which tokens appear; discarded entirely by set (bag) models.

connections: p.422: set models discard token order and convert each review to an unordered bag of tokens

paragraphs.excerpt: Therefore, it is usually a good idea to inject some knowledge of local word ordering
paragraphs.what_it_says: Even set-based models benefit from some knowledge of local word order. An easy way is bigrams, two consecutive tokens. For "this movie made me cry", the unigrams are {"this", "movie", "made", "me", "cry"} and the bigrams are {"this movie", "movie made", "made me", "me cry"}. The bag-of-words model is equivalently a unigram model, and an n-gram is an ordered sequence of n tokens.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The input is still a *set*, but its elements are now richer. Each bigram records that two specific words were adjacent and in that order ("made me" differs from "me made"). A sentence of L tokens has L unigrams and L-1 bigrams, so the five-word example gives 4 bigrams.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces the n-gram vocabulary used for the rest of section 14.4 and makes clear that the earlier model is the n = 1 special case.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Number of n-grams in a sequence of length L: $L - n + 1$. For L = 5: 5 unigrams, 4 bigrams, 3 trigrams.

terminology.meaning: A single token; a bag-of-words model is a unigram model.
Two tokens that appear consecutively in the input text.
An ordered sequence of n consecutive tokens, for any n.

connections: p.422: the same example sentence "this movie made me cry" was used to illustrate the bag-of-words encoding

paragraphs.excerpt: To add bigrams to our model, we want to consider the frequency of all bigrams
paragraphs.what_it_says: Bigram frequencies must be counted when building the vocabulary. There are two options: a vocabulary of only bigrams, or one where unigrams and bigrams compete for space. In the latter, "United States" enters the vocabulary before "ventriloquism" if it occurs more often in the input.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Vocabulary building means ranking candidate terms by frequency and keeping the top max_tokens. In the shared scheme, a frequent bigram can push out a rare unigram, so the vocabulary keeps whatever terms are most common regardless of length.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The vocabulary is a fixed budget (30,000 slots in listing 14.16). Deciding how unigrams and bigrams share it determines which features the linear model can use.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: TextVectorization's adapt() counts all requested n-grams together and keeps the most frequent ones, which is the "compete for space" option. With ngrams=2 that pool contains both unigrams and bigrams. Note that the default standardization lowercases text and strips punctuation, so the actual vocabulary entry would be "united states".

terminology.meaning: The fixed list of terms that get their own index; terms outside it map to the OOV/[UNK] index.

connections: p.423: a 20,000-word vocabulary was learned with adapt() for the unigram model

paragraphs.excerpt: Again, we could build this by extending our WordTokenizer from earlier in the chapter
paragraphs.what_it_says: The WordTokenizer from earlier in the chapter could be extended, but there is no need: TextVectorization does it out of the box. The authors train a slightly larger vocabulary to account for bigrams, adapt() a new vocabulary, and multi-hot encode output vectors that include bigrams.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Three changes from listing 14.12: a larger vocabulary (30,000 instead of 20,000), the ngrams=2 option, and a fresh adapt() call, because the old vocabulary contains no bigrams.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that a library preprocessing layer can replace a hand-written tokenizer, and that a larger feature space needs a larger vocabulary budget.

terminology.meaning: Method of Keras preprocessing layers that learns layer state (here, the vocabulary) from data.
A vector of length max_tokens with 1 at the index of every vocabulary term present in the input.

connections: p.423: TextVectorization handles word and character tokenization and multi-hot output
p.428: a batch of the new encoding has shape (32, 30000)

concepts.name: n-gram
concepts.definition: An ordered sequence of n consecutive tokens; unigrams (n=1) and bigrams (n=2) are the common cases.
concepts.intuition: Gluing neighbouring words into a single feature so the model can see short phrases.
concepts.technical: A sequence of L tokens has L-n+1 n-grams. With ngrams=2, TextVectorization emits all unigrams and all bigrams, which are then looked up in a shared vocabulary.
concepts.significance: Adds local word order to set models cheaply; raises IMDb test accuracy from 88% to 90% (p.428).
concepts.example: "this movie made me cry" -> bigrams {"this movie", "movie made", "made me", "me cry"}.
concepts.misconception: That ngrams=2 yields only bigrams. Per the listing's callout, it considers all unigrams and bigrams.

concepts.name: Bag-of-words (unigram) model
concepts.definition: A set model whose features are single tokens; the bag-of-words model just trained can equivalently be called a unigram model.
concepts.intuition: Each word votes independently, whatever its neighbours.
concepts.technical: Multi-hot over a word vocabulary + a Dense(1, sigmoid) layer.
concepts.example: "not bad" gets w(not) + w(bad), which is probably negative overall.
concepts.misconception: That it captures phrases. It cannot distinguish "not bad" from "bad ... not".

concepts.name: Multi-hot encoding with n-grams
concepts.definition: A binary vector of length max_tokens marking which vocabulary terms (unigrams and bigrams here) occur in the input.
concepts.intuition: A checklist of 30,000 terms, ticked if present.
concepts.technical: output_mode="multi_hot" in TextVectorization; batch shape becomes (32, 30000) (p.428).
concepts.significance: Lets the unchanged linear classifier use bigram features.
concepts.example: A review containing "not bad" ticks the index of "not", of "bad" and of "not bad" (if all are in the vocabulary).
concepts.misconception: That multi-hot counts occurrences. It only records presence (count mode would record frequency).

math.title: Counting n-grams in a sentence
math.source_text: Not printed as a formula; illustrated by the 5 unigrams and 4 bigrams of "this movie made me cry".

variables.meaning: number of tokens in the sequence

math.operations: Slide a window of n consecutive tokens across the sequence.
math.purpose: Shows how many extra features bigrams add per review (about one per word).
math.interpretation: With ngrams=2 a review produces about 2L candidate terms (L unigrams + L-1 bigrams) before deduplication and vocabulary lookup.
math.intuition: Every adjacent pair of words is one bigram.
math.numerical_example: L = 5 ("this movie made me cry"): unigrams 5 - 1 + 1 = 5, bigrams 5 - 2 + 1 = 4, matching the sets printed on the page.

code.title: Applying a bigram encoding to the IMDb reviews
code.original_code:
max_tokens = 30_000
text_vectorization = layers.TextVectorization(
    max_tokens=max_tokens,
    split="whitespace",
    output_mode="multi_hot",
    ngrams=2,
)
text_vectorization.adapt(train_ds_no_labels)
bigram_train_ds = train_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
bigram_val_ds = val_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
bigram_test_ds = test_ds.map(
    lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8
)
code.what_it_does: Creates a new TextVectorization layer whose vocabulary holds the 30,000 most frequent unigrams and bigrams, learns that vocabulary from the training texts, and builds train/validation/test datasets of multi-hot vectors including bigram features.

line_explanations.explanation: Vocabulary budget raised from 20,000 (listing 14.12) to 30,000 to make room for bigrams.
The layer splits on whitespace (callout: "Learns a word-level vocabulary"), outputs multi-hot vectors, and with ngrams=2 "considers all unigrams and bigrams" (callout).
adapt() iterates over train_ds_no_labels (the texts only, defined on p.423 as train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x)) and counts term frequencies to build the new vocabulary. Only training data is used.
Each split is mapped through the layer, keeping labels unchanged; num_parallel_calls=8 vectorizes batches on 8 CPU threads, the tf.data parallelism discussed in the sidebar on p.426.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: datasets of (batch of review strings, labels). Output: datasets of (float multi-hot tensor of shape (batch, 30000), labels); p.428 shows a batch of shape (32, 30000).
code.algorithm: Standardize (default lower_and_strip_punctuation) -> split on whitespace -> generate unigrams and bigrams -> look up each in the vocabulary -> set 1 at each found index.
code.theory_link: Implements the shared unigram + bigram vocabulary described in the text, where both kinds of term compete by frequency.

parameters.name: max_tokens
parameters.role: vocabulary size, including the reserved OOV entry; also the length of each multi-hot vector

parameters.name: split
parameters.role: how to split standardized text into tokens (whitespace = words)

parameters.name: ngrams
parameters.role: 2 = emit all n-grams up to 2 (unigrams and bigrams); a tuple such as (2,) would select specific orders

parameters.name: num_parallel_calls
parameters.role: number of parallel CPU calls in tf.data map

pitfalls: Re-running adapt() is essential: the vocabulary from listing 14.12 contains no bigrams.
The variable text_vectorization is overwritten, so any earlier dataset built with the old layer must not be re-mapped with this one by mistake.
max_tokens also sets the model input size; the classifier must be rebuilt with 30,000 inputs (done on p.428).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: see what ngrams=2 produces for one sentence
from keras import layers
tv = layers.TextVectorization(output_mode="int", ngrams=2)
tv.adapt(["this movie made me cry"])
print(tv.get_vocabulary())
# contains '[UNK]', the 5 unigrams and the 4 bigrams such as 'this movie'

deeper.title: Why "not bad" breaks a unigram model
deeper.body: Suppose a trained unigram model has $w_{\text{not}} = -0.4$ and $w_{\text{bad}} = -1.5$. The phrase "not bad" contributes $-1.9$ to the logit: strongly negative. A bigram model also has $w_{\text{not bad}}$, which training can set to, say, $+2.2$, so the total becomes $-0.4 - 1.5 + 2.2 = +0.3$: mildly positive, as a human would read it. The numbers are illustrative, not from the book.

deeper.title: Two ways to build an n-gram vocabulary
deeper.body:
- **Bigrams only**: all slots go to word pairs. This captures phrases, but common single words that appear in no frequent bigram are lost.
- **Unigrams and bigrams compete** (what `ngrams=2` does): one ranked list by frequency. Frequent phrases like "united states" beat rare words like "ventriloquism". This is why the vocabulary grows to 30,000: about 10,000 extra slots for the most frequent bigrams, while still keeping common words.

deeper.title: Phrase stickers
deeper.body: A unigram model reads a review as a pile of single-word stickers. A bigram model also gets stickers for every pair of neighbouring words. It still doesn't know the full order of the pile, but each phrase sticker preserves a little local order.

takeaways: Discarding all word order loses multi-word meaning such as "United States" and "not bad".
Bigrams (pairs of consecutive tokens) add local order while keeping the simple set model.
The bag-of-words model is a unigram model; an n-gram is an ordered sequence of n tokens.
Unigrams and bigrams can share one vocabulary and compete for slots by frequency.
Listing 14.16 only changes max_tokens to 30,000, adds ngrams=2 and re-adapts the vocabulary.

questions.question: List the bigrams of "this movie made me cry".
questions.explanation: Bigrams are the pairs of consecutive tokens; a five-token sentence has 5 - 2 + 1 = 4 of them, as printed on the page.

questions.question: What does setting ngrams=2 in listing 14.16 do?
options: Keeps only bigrams in the vocabulary
Considers all unigrams and bigrams as vocabulary candidates
Splits each word into two-character pieces
questions.answer: Considers all unigrams and bigrams as vocabulary candidates
questions.explanation: The callout on the listing says "Considers all unigrams and bigrams". Bigrams are word pairs, not character pieces, and the vocabulary size is set explicitly by max_tokens=30_000.

questions.question: Why should "not bad" and "bad" get different sentiment scores, and why can a unigram model not achieve this cleanly?
questions.answer: "Not" reverses the meaning of "bad". A unigram model adds independent word weights, so "not bad" scores w(not) + w(bad), still dominated by the negative "bad". A bigram feature gives the phrase its own weight.
questions.explanation: The page uses this example to argue that discarding all word order is very reductive.

questions.question: Why was max_tokens raised from 20,000 to 30,000?
questions.answer: To account for bigrams, which compete with unigrams for vocabulary slots; a larger vocabulary keeps the common words while adding frequent phrases.
questions.explanation: The text: "We will train a slightly larger vocabulary to account for the presence of bigrams."

questions.question: In a vocabulary where unigrams and bigrams compete for space, when does "United States" enter before "ventriloquism"?
options: If it occurs more frequently in the input text
Only if the vocabulary is bigram-only
questions.answer: If it occurs more frequently in the input text
questions.explanation: Terms are ranked by frequency regardless of n-gram order. Neither type has priority, and the bigram-only scheme wouldn't contain "ventriloquism" at all.

questions.question: A review has 200 tokens. How many unigrams and bigrams (with repeats) does TextVectorization(ngrams=2) generate before vocabulary lookup?
questions.explanation: There are L - n + 1 n-grams per order. The multi-hot vector then records only which distinct terms are present in the vocabulary.

questions.question: Could you rewrite listing 14.12 into listing 14.16 from memory, naming each change and why it is needed?
questions.answer: max_tokens 20,000 -> 30,000 (room for bigrams); add ngrams=2 (generate bigrams); re-run adapt() (a new vocabulary that contains bigrams); rename the datasets bigram_*.
questions.explanation: Everything else (split, multi_hot, parallel map) stays the same, which is what makes the comparison with the unigram model fair.
